name: Iquito
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Iquito (iqui1243) is not in the catalog. All four sweep items are about Iquito word stress. Three were fetched sources open and read: Michael 2011 (Amerindia 35, journal site) is the authoritative first-hand statement — quantity-sensitive right-to-left moraic trochees, primary stress on the rightmost foot (penult in...LL, final if heavy), all heavy syllables stressed, left-edge degenerate feet only to make a dipodic word, stress diagnosed by post-tonic consonant lengthening and separated from a low-density H/ø tone system whose default H docks on the stressed syllable. Sullón Acosta 2005 (UNMSM thesis, recovered via the DSpace 7 backend at handle 20.500.12672/1230; Glottolog's URL is dead) equates 'primary stress' with the pitch peak and so places it toward the left edge (LEFTMOST ranking) with penultimate 'secondary stress'; Michael 2011 p. 71 rejects that premise, and her right-to-left footing and penultimate prominence agree with his analysis once pitch is reassigned to tone. Topintzi 2017 (ISTAL 22, open) is a Harmonic-Serialism reanalysis of Michael's data with no new data ('leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress'); it points to a fuller chapter, Topintzi 2016 in Dimensions of Phonological Stress (CUP, paywalled, not in the item list). Michael 2010 (Berkeley PLAR) could not be fetched sources (eScholarship WAF; Internet Archive offline) and is presumably the prepublication of the 2011 article — low priority. Suggested coding: fixed rightmost-foot (penultimate/final) quantity-sensitive trochaic stress with a separate lexical tone system. all discovery was by direct fetch.

new_statements.quote: For the most part, the Iquito stress system is relatively simple, consisting of right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees. The language generally does not permit degenerate feet. The language is quantity sensitive, with C(y)V: syllables counting as heavy (recall that the language does not exhibit closed syllables). [p. 57] ... Turning to words containing heavy syllables, we find that all heavy syllables are stressed in Iquito, and that the stress pattern in such words shows that heavy syllables form their own foot. This indicates that the trochees in the language are moraic, and not syllabic. [p. 58]
new_statements.citation: Michael, Lev (2011). The interaction of tone and stress in the prosodic system of Iquito (Zaparoan). Amerindia 35: 53-74.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (22-page PDF, text layer;.txt beside it). new_statements.rule_in_words: Feet are bimoraic trochees built from the right edge of the prosodic word; the head of the rightmost foot carries primary stress. So primary stress is penultimate when the last two syllables are light (ˈa.ʃi, ku.ma.ˈki.ha), final when the final syllable has a long vowel (nu.ta.ku.ˈrɨɨ), and on a heavy penult before a light final (ˈsaa.pi, trimoraic foot rather than a final degenerate foot). Every long-vowel syllable is stressed. Primary stress carries a default high tone when the word has no lexical tone in its rightmost colon; the acoustic correlate of stress itself is lengthening of the post-tonic consonant, not pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: exhaustive right-to-left parsing gives secondary stress on the head of every non-final foot, e.g. (ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura), (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ). A single light syllable at the left edge is normally left unparsed, but is parsed into a degenerate secondary-stressed foot when that makes the word dipodic: (ˌka)(ˈha.ʃi) 'hair', (ˌma)(ˈhuu). Degenerate feet are never permitted at the right edge (*(ˌL)(ˈL), *(ˌH)(ˈL)).
new_statements.exceptions: Trimoraic feet (ˈHL) at the right edge; degenerate initial feet in trisyllabic/dipodic words. Michael notes Sullón (2005) analyzed the same data with primary stress on the leftmost foot by equating primary stress with the pitch peak, and Eastman & Eastman (1963) posited tone but no stress; he attributes both to conflating pitch with stress. The 2019/2022 dictionaries report a revised tonal analysis (H/L/null, HLL melodies) but do not revise the stress statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic word, defined (fn. 1, p. 66) as the domain of stress and tone assignment and the unit subject to the bimoraic minimum; monomoraic pronouns and negation cliticize into the host's prosodic word (nu=makii, ka=tɨ=ʃiipa). Transcriptions are non-prepausal citation forms (prepausal final-vowel devoicing and long-vowel shortening do not affect stress). Data from San Antonio de Pintuyacu speakers, 2002-2008; stress established by tapping tasks plus post-tonic consonant duration.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Iquito of San Antonio de Pintuyacu (Pintuyacu River, Loreto), the only community with fluent speakers; language-level iqui1243. Michael 2011 (p. 54) notes Kawarano, sometimes listed separately, is considered a dialect of Iquito by speakers.

new_statements.quote: For the most part, the Iquito stress system is relatively simple, consisting of right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees. The language generally does not permit degenerate feet. The language is quantity sensitive, with C(y)V: syllables counting as heavy (recall that the language does not exhibit closed syllables). [...] (5) a. (ˈLL) i. (ˈa.ʃi) [...] c. (ˌLL)(ˈLL) i. (ˌku.ma)(ˈki.ha) [...] d. L(ˌLL)(ˈLL) i. nu(ˌtaki)(ˈnaka) [...] (6) a. nu(ˌta.ku)(ˈrɨɨ) 's/he stood up' [...] all heavy syllables are stressed in Iquito, and [...] heavy syllables form their own foot.
new_statements.citation: Michael, Lev (2011). The interaction of tone and stress in the prosodic system of Iquito (Zaparoan). Amerindia 35: 53-74.
new_statements.reading: Quantity-sensitive, right-to-left moraic trochees with primary stress on the rightmost foot: penultimate syllable in words ending in two light syllables, final syllable when it is heavy (CV:); every heavy syllable is stressed; secondary stress on alternating preceding feet; a left-edge degenerate foot only when it makes the word dipodic, never at the right edge; (ˈHL) trimoraic foot rather than a final degenerate foot. Stress is diagnosed by tapping judgments and post-tonic consonant lengthening, independent of the H/ø tone system, whose default (metrical) H falls on the primary-stressed syllable in toneless words. First-hand fieldwork by the ILDP lead linguist; explicitly supersedes Sullón 2005's pitch-based analysis.

sources.citation: Michael, Lev (2011). The interaction of tone and stress in the prosodic system of Iquito (Zaparoan, Peru). Amerindia 35: 53-74.
sources.quote: For the most part, the Iquito stress system is relatively simple, consisting of right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees. The language generally does not permit degenerate feet. The language is quantity sensitive, with C(y)V: syllables counting as heavy (recall that the language does not exhibit closed syllables). [p. 57] ... Turning to words containing heavy syllables, we find that all heavy syllables are stressed in Iquito, and that the stress pattern in such words shows that heavy syllables form their own foot. This indicates that the trochees in the language are moraic, and not syllabic. [p. 58]
sources.note: §4 (pp. 57-61): right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees, quantity-sensitive (CV: heavy, no codas), primary stress on the rightmost foot, all heavy syllables stressed, degenerate initial foot only to make a dipodic word; acoustic correlate is post-tonic consonant lengthening, not pitch; §5: privative H tone system, a metrical H is assigned to the primary-stressed syllable when the rightmost colon has no lexical tone.

sources.citation: Sullón Acosta, Karina Natalia (2005). El acento y tono en la lengua Iquito. Tesis de Licenciatura, Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, Lima. vi+97 pp. (110 pp. PDF).
sources.quote: p. 4: 'a. El acento primario recae sobre la sílaba que esté más a la izquierda de la palabra prosódica, siempre y cuando la sílaba que le sigue sea ligera. b. Acentúese la segunda sílaba si ésta es pesada. En el caso de palabras de tres y cuatro sílabas asígnese el acento en la segunda sílaba, siempre y cuando la primera sílaba sea ligera. c. Asígnese el acento sobre la tercera sílaba en el caso de palabras de cinco sílabas, siempre y cuando las dos anteriores sean ligeras.' p. 87: 'El pitch alto es un rasgo de acento primario en iquito y éste se asigna mediante la formación de pies desde el margen derecho de la palabra. No obstante, la cabeza de la palabra prosódica es el pie que está más a la izquierda.' [Translation: a. Primary stress falls on the leftmost syllable of the prosodic word provided the following syllable is light. b. Stress the second syllable if it is heavy; in three- and four-syllable words assign stress to the second syllable provided the first is light. c. Assign stress to the third syllable in five-syllable words whenever the two preceding ones are light. / High pitch is a feature of primary stress in Iquito and it is assigned by foot formation from the right…
sources.locator: Resumen p. 4 (PDF p. 10); §4.4.1.1 pp. 55-56 (PDF pp. 61-62); Conclusiones p. 87 (PDF p. 93)
sources.note: Resumen pp. 2-7 and §4.4 pp. 54-60: two prominences per word (one near the left edge, one penultimate); takes high pitch as the correlate of primary stress, so primary stress falls on the leftmost foot (first syllable if the next is light; second syllable if heavy or in 3-4 syllable words with light first syllable; third syllable in 5-syllable words), secondary stress always penultimate; a 'fourth pattern' with initial stress regardless of weight, attributed to a lexical low tone; verbs stress the heavy root syllable. Michael 2011 §6 (p. 71) rejects this pitch-based analysis.

sources.citation: Topintzi, Nina (2017). The prosodic colon in stress, tone and prosodic templates: Evidence from Iquito and elsewhere. Selected Papers of ISTAL 22: 466-479.
sources.quote: Iquito, a Zaparoan language of Peru (all data come from Michael 2011) is a low-density tonal language that displays both stress and tone. [...] Iquito parses feet into leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress. These can either contain a single heavy syllable (H) or two light ones (LL). [...] Iquito normally bans degenerate (L) feet [...] In odd-parity words [...] the extra syllable at the left edge of the word remains unparsed.
sources.note: Secondary (all data from Michael 2011): 'Iquito parses feet into leftward bimoraic trochees with rightmost primary stress' (p. 468); Harmonic Serialism analysis of the degenerate-foot/colon facts.

sources.note: No phonology chapter (TOC: theory, methodology, basic constructions, TAM); orthography note p. 14 only says 'the pitch-accent (also referred to as tone by the ILDP) is also marked on the vowel' and that tone analysis is a developing project; nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Michael, Lev; Beier, Christine; Pacaya Inuma, Jaime; et al. (2022). Diccionario iquito-castellano. ILDP / Cabeceras Aid Project.
sources.note: Section 'El tono' (p. 19): three tonal values H/L/null, HLL melodies, floating tones, boundary tones; tone now marked with acute and grave. 'Acento' appears only as the name of the diacritics; no statement about stress.

sources.citation: Michael, Lev; Beier, Christine; Pacaya Inuma, Jaime; et al. (2019). Iquito-English Dictionary. ILDP / Cabeceras Aid Project.
sources.note: §1.1.2 'Tone graphemes and orthography' (pp. 4-5): tonal inventory H, L, null; most tones are part of an HLL melody; only H marked. Preface (pp. xiii-xv) says the prosodic analysis has advanced since 2011 and a descriptive grammar is in preparation. No statement about stress.
